reference.source: Bárány Society and International Headache Society diagnostic criteria for vestibular migraine
clinicalPearls: The commonest cause of recurrent spontaneous vertigo and a frequently under-recognised diagnosis; it should be considered in any patient with episodic vestibular symptoms and a migraine history.
Vertigo need not be temporally linked to headache — episodes may occur with, before, after, or entirely without cephalgia, which is a common reason the diagnosis is missed.

Attack phenomenology is highly variable: spontaneous or positional vertigo, head-motion intolerance, or internal/external illusory movement, lasting anywhere from a few minutes to as long as a few days.
Diagnosis requires a current or past history of migraine plus migrainous features (migraine-type headache, photophobia, phonophobia, or visual aura) during at least half of the vestibular episodes.
Interictal examination is usually normal, although subtle central oculomotor signs such as gaze-evoked or positional nystagmus of central type may be present.
It overlaps and may coexist with Menière's disease and benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, and can evolve into persistent postural-perceptual dizziness.
Osmophobia, visual aura, and a family history of migraine strengthen the diagnosis; triggers mirror those of migraine (sleep disturbance, stress, hormonal fluctuation, dietary and sensory stimuli).

Management combines trigger avoidance and lifestyle measures with migraine prophylaxis (beta-blockers, tricyclic antidepressants, anticonvulsants, or calcium-channel blockers) rather than long-term vestibular sedatives.
reference.pathophysiology: The mechanism is incompletely understood but is thought to arise from the same trigeminovascular and central sensory-processing dysfunction that underlies migraine, applied to vestibular pathways. Reciprocal anatomical connections link trigeminal nociceptive neurones with central vestibular nuclei, and neuropeptides such as calcitonin gene-related peptide modulate vestibular processing. Cortical spreading depression, thalamocortical dysrhythmia, and transient dysfunction of central multisensory integration are all implicated, producing episodic mismatch between vestibular, visual, and proprioceptive signals. A strong genetic predisposition exists, and channelopathy genes (notably CACNA1A, shared with familial hemiplegic migraine and episodic ataxia type 2) illustrate the mechanistic overlap between migraine and paroxysmal vestibular disorders.
additionalDifferentials: posterior circulation transient ischaemic attack or stroke
additionalInvestigations: pure-tone audiometry to exclude the fluctuating low-frequency loss of Menière's disease
video head impulse testing and caloric testing (typically normal or non-lateralising interictally)
cervical and ocular vestibular evoked myogenic potentials
MRI of the brain and internal auditory meati to exclude structural or central pathology
orthostatic blood pressure measurement to exclude an orthostatic contribution
structured headache and vertigo diary to demonstrate the temporal relationship of migrainous features
redFlags: acute severe vertigo accompanied by brainstem signs (dysarthria, diplopia, limb ataxia, sensory loss) suggesting posterior circulation stroke
progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss or persistent unilateral tinnitus suggesting retrocochlear pathology or Menière's disease
first presentation of vestibular symptoms in an older patient with vascular risk factors
new persistent headache with focal neurological deficit or papilloedema
reference.prognosis: Vestibular migraine typically follows a chronic relapsing-remitting course that fluctuates over years and often improves with prophylaxis and lifestyle modification. A proportion of patients develop chronic dizziness or secondary persistent postural-perceptual dizziness if untreated.
pitfalls: attributing all episodic vertigo to migraine without excluding Menière's disease or benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
expecting headache to accompany every attack and therefore rejecting the diagnosis when vertigo occurs in isolation
over-relying on normal interictal vestibular tests, which do not exclude the diagnosis
missing a coexisting benign paroxysmal positional vertigo that is independently treatable
long-term use of vestibular suppressants, which impair central compensation and may perpetuate symptoms

management: Trigger identification and lifestyle modification with regular sleep, hydration, consistent meals and reduction of dietary and stress triggers as first-line preventive management
Migraine preventive pharmacotherapy such as beta-blockers, amitriptyline, topiramate or flunarizine for frequent or disabling attacks
Acute attack treatment with triptans and antiemetics, using vestibular suppressants only briefly to avoid impairing central compensation
Vestibular rehabilitation exercises for persistent imbalance and motion sensitivity
Maintain a structured headache and vertigo diary to track attacks, triggers and treatment response
Address comorbid anxiety and coexisting Menière's disease or benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
Refer to neuro-otology and escalate if the course is atypical or progresses toward persistent postural-perceptual dizziness
